'''Windsor Terrace''' is a small residential neighborhood in the central part of the [[New York City]] [[Boroughs of New York City|borough]] of [[Brooklyn]].<ref name=":10" /> It is bounded by [[Prospect Park, Brooklyn|Prospect Park]] on the east and northeast, [[Park Slope]] at Prospect Park West, [[Green-Wood Cemetery]], and [[Borough Park, Brooklyn|Borough Park]] at McDonald Avenue on the northwest, west, and southwest, and [[Kensington, Brooklyn|Kensington]] at Caton Avenue on the south. As of the [[2010 United States census]], Windsor Terrace had 20,988 people living within its {{Convert|0.503|mi2|km2|adj=on}} area.

Windsor Terrace is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 7|Brooklyn Community District 7]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]]s are 11215 and 11218.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 72nd Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 72nd Precinct"/> Fire services are provided by Engine Company 240/Battalion 48 of the [[New York City Fire Department]]. Politically, Windsor Terrace is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 38th and 39th Districts.

==History==
Before the coming of Europeans to the New World, the area which is now Windsor Terrace was inhabited by the [[Canarsee Indians]].<ref name="Internet Archive 2006">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924088998061|title=The civil, political, professional and ecclesiastical history, and commercial and industrial record of the county of Kings and the city of Brooklyn, N. Y., from 1683 to 1884|publisher=W.W. Munsell|year=1884|editor-last=Stiles|editor-first=Henry Reed|location=[[New York City|New York]]|pages=230–235|via=Internet Archive|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Israelowitz-LinderZacharias-Ditmas">See:

*{{cite book|title=Brooklyn's Windsor Terrace, Kensington, & Parkville Communities|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bPrwZwEACAAJ|year=2010|publisher=Israelowitz Publishing|isbn=978-1-878741-90-5}}
*{{cite book|author1=Marc Linder|author2=Lawrence Zacharias|title=Of cabbages and Kings County: agriculture and the formation of modern Brooklyn|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZqR4AAAAMAAJ|date=May 1, 1999|publisher=University of Iowa Press|isbn=9780877456704}}
*{{cite book|author=Charles Andrew Ditmas|title=Historic Homesteads of Kings County ...|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Q3pEAQAAMAAJ|year=1909|publisher=The Compiler}}
</ref><ref name="brookneighb" /> Specifically, the Gowanus and Werpos tribes inhabited the surrounding area.<ref name="Internet Archive 2006" /><ref name="Israelowitz-LinderZacharias-Ditmas" /><ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}} The land, which was then in the far northwestern corner of the [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Town of Flatbush]],<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}} was purchased as a farm by [[John Vanderbilt]].<ref name="Israelowitz-LinderZacharias-Ditmas" /><ref name=":0"/><ref name=gotham933/> Some parts of the land were also maintained by the Martense family, who owned land in the area through 1895.<ref name=":13" /> This area was desirable due to its proximity to [[downtown Brooklyn]], as well as the recent construction of the [[Coney Island Avenue|Coney Island Plank Road]] through the area and of the serene [[Green-Wood Cemetery]] to the southwest.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50368470/|title=Brooklyn Daily Eagle - 23 March 1854|date=March 23, 1854|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=October 10, 2016|via=[[newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

Following Vanderbilt's death, his land was divided in two.<ref name="Israelowitz-LinderZacharias-Ditmas" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name="gotham933" /> Vanderbilt's land were sold to William Bell, a real estate developer, in 1849.<ref name="Internet Archive 2006" /><ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2007/03/windsor-terrace-brooklyn/|title=WINDSOR TERRACE, Brooklyn — Forgotten New York|website=forgotten-ny.com|access-date=October 10, 2016}}</ref> Bell subdivided the land into 47 building lots,<ref name="brookneighb" /> and, unlike some other developers in the general area, was able to sell them rather quickly.<ref name="gotham933">{{cite gotham}}, p.933</ref> Bell then renamed the area after one of the multiple places named Windsor in England.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://theweeklynabe.com/2012/04/18/windsor-terrace-brooklyn-history/|title=Windsor Terrace: a river of cars runs through it|last=Williams|first=Keith|website=The Weekly Nabe|access-date=October 10, 2016|archive-date=October 22, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161022072944/http://theweeklynabe.com/2012/04/18/windsor-terrace-brooklyn-history/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bell sold part of the land to Edward Belknap in 1851, and Belknap subsequently built four streets on which he marked 49 lots for future "Pleasant Cottages."<ref name=":13" /> The development was incorporated as the Village of Windsor Terrace, which was bounded by Church Avenue on the south, [[McDonald Avenue]] on the west, the Brooklyn–Flatbush town line on the north, and Prospect Park Southwest and Coney Island Avenue on the east.<ref name="Internet Archive 2006" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~217388~5503569:Parkville,-Flatbush--Windsor-Terrac?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort,Pub_Date,Pub_List_No,Series_No&qvq=q:Parkville;sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort,Pub_Date,Pub_List_No,Series_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=0&trs=1|title=Parkville, Flatbush. Windsor Terrace, Flatbush. Bath, New Long Island. Utrecht. New Utrecht. - David Rumsey Historical Map Collection|website=www.davidrumsey.com|access-date=October 10, 2016}}</ref>  The [[Brooklyn Eagle|''Brooklyn Daily Eagle'']] first referred to the area as "Windsor Terrace" in March 1854.<ref name="Internet Archive 2006" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50368316/|title=Brooklyn Daily Eagle - 18 March 1854|date=March 18, 1854|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=October 10, 2016|via=[[newspapers.com]]}}</ref> By 1856, Belknap had lost his land due to foreclosure.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Foreclosure-Supreme Court, County of Kings|date=September 30, 1856|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|page=4}}</ref>

The area was generally desirable due to its prime location in the far northwest of the Town of Flatbush; close to the City of Brooklyn, yet located far enough outside it that residents of Windsor Terrace were willing to move there for its suburban ambience;<ref name=":0" /> and within walking distance of the [[B68 (New York City bus)|Coney Island and Brooklyn Railroad's horsecar line]].<ref>{{cite news |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=FA0F17FC345B1B7493C1AB178DD85F468684F9 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120717193145/http://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=FA0F17FC345B1B7493C1AB178DD85F468684F9 |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 17, 2012 |title=Brooklyn News |date=June 23, 1862 }}</ref> Additional blocks were developed in 1862,<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name="encnyc" /> when the village had 30 inhabitants living in twelve houses.<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}} The village kept growing through the 1870s,<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}} boasting a Protestant chapel by 1874,<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}} a public school by 1876,<ref name="Internet Archive 2006" /><ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}}<ref name="encnyc" /> and its own volunteer fire department by 1888.<ref name="Internet Archive 2006" /><ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name="encnyc" /><ref name=":11">{{cite web|url=http://nyfd.com/brooklyn_engines/engine_240/engine_240.pdf|title=WINDSOR TERRACE AND ENGINE 240|last1=Boucher|first1=Mike|last2=Van Holt|first2=Donald|website=nyfd.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> The village remained rural in feel until around 1900, when row houses began to be built throughout the area, at first along Prospect Park SW.<ref name=":10">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/08/realestate/windsor-terrace-less-way-station-more-destination.html|title=Windsor Terrace: Less Way Station, More Destination|last=Hughes|first=C. J.|date=December 3, 2013|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref>

Development began to pick up pace during the 1920s as rumors circulated that the neighborhood would soon be served by the [[New York City Subway]]. There were a lot of single-family and two-family houses being built, as well as stores being opened on 11th Avenue and two apartment buildings being erected on [[Prospect Avenue (Brooklyn)|Prospect Avenue]].<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2–3 }}  Many of the new occupants of Windsor Terrace were Irish-Americans, many of whose families remain there to this day.<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name="encnyc" /> The 1933 arrival of the [[Independent Subway System]] (IND) ushered in an era of apartment-building construction.<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2–3}}

Even into the 1960s, Windsor Terrace was an isolated neighborhood with a quiet small-town feel to it, although the construction of the Prospect Expressway brought more through-traffic past the area. [[Gentrification]] of the neighborhood began in the 1980s, with families who could not afford the prices in [[Brooklyn Heights]] and [[Park Slope]] coming to Windsor Terrace instead, looking for more affordable real estate.<ref name=brookneighb /><ref name=encnyc /> During this time, the old square block-sized Pilgrim Laundry, site of an ancient Victorian-era brick edifice at the corner of Prospect Avenue and Terrace Place, was razed and replaced with 17 two-family houses constructed in 1983. The houses were funded with the cooperation of a public-private partnership and sold through lottery to locals. This brought attention to the need for affordable housing in Brooklyn, and in the late 1980s, the neighborhood was rezoned to prevent the construction of high-rise buildings in order to retain the small-town fabric of the existing neighborhood.<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name="encnyc" /> However, by then, [[gentrification]] of the neighborhood had started, and would continue through the 2000s.<ref name=":10"/><ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" />

Residents protested after [[Key Food]], the only major supermarket in the neighborhood, closed down in 2015. A new, smaller Key Food-owned store called Windsor Farms Market was opened and is currently operating in a portion of the old location.<ref name=NYT022715/> A [[food co-op]] called "Windsor Terrace Food Coop", using the model of the [[Park Slope Food Coop]], was also organized at the same time.<ref name="NYT022715">{{cite news|last=Miller, Stuart|title=In Brooklyn, First Comes Gentrification, Then Comes a Food Co-op|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/03/01/nyregion/a-new-food-co-op-in-brooklyn-centered-on-community-joins-the-hub.html|access-date=March 1, 2015|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=February 27, 2015}}</ref> The co-op serves both as a supplier of food and a community focal point. To become a member, residents must pay a one-time fee and commit to a work requirement, although memberships from other Brooklyn food co-ops are honored. The food, especially produce, is often higher quality and lower in price than at local supermarkets.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://windsorterracefoodcoop.com/ |title=Welcome to Windsor Terrace Food Coop! |website=windsorterracefoodcoop.com |access-date=July 21, 2019}}</ref><ref name=NYT022715/>

==Location and street grid==

===Boundaries===
[[File:WindsorTerraceStreet.JPG|thumb|right|upright=1.2|Typical residential street in Windsor Terrace]]

Windsor Terrace, which is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 7|Community Board 7]],<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www1.nyc.gov/site/brooklyncb7/index.page|title=Brooklyn Community Board 7|website=www1.nyc.gov|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> consists of a narrow, nine-block-wide area.<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite news|url=http://www.villagevoice.com/news/close-up-on-windsor-terrace-6408943|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161012080506/http://www.villagevoice.com/news/close-up-on-windsor-terrace-6408943|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 12, 2016|title=Close-Up on Windsor Terrace|last=Ashman|first=Angela|date=October 28, 2003|newspaper=Village Voice|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Located in central Brooklyn, the neighborhood has a "curved, somewhat comma-like shape".<ref name=":10" /> The neighborhood lies between Green-Wood Cemetery to the southwest and [[Prospect Park (Brooklyn)|Prospect Park]] to the northeast, split down the middle by the [[New York State Route 27|Prospect Expressway]].<ref name=":1" /> Adjacent neighborhoods include Park Slope to the northeast and [[Kensington, Brooklyn|Kensington]] to the south.<ref name="brookneighb" /> According to ''The Neighborhoods of Brooklyn'', Windsor Terrace is bounded by Prospect Park West on the north, Prospect Park SW and Coney Island Avenue on the east, Caton Avenue on the south and McDonald Avenue on the west.<ref name="brookneighb">"Windsor Terrace" in {{cite brookneighb}}, pp.212-214</ref> However, the ''Encyclopedia of New York City'' gives the boundaries as Seventh Avenue and Prospect Park W on the north, Prospect Park SW to the east, and Green-Wood Cemetery to the south and west.<ref name="encnyc">Gallagher, John J. "Windsor Terrace" in {{cite enc-nyc2}}, p.1405</ref> Other sources extend the northwest corner to Eighth Avenue along 15th Street and 20th Street.<ref>[https://www.google.com/maps/place/Windsor+Terrace,+Brooklyn,+NY/@40.6568755,-73.9764243,15z/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x89c25b21e9b80a2d:0xb69448ccb009be06 "Windsor Terrace"] [[Google Maps]]  Accessed:February 26, 2015</ref>

Windsor Terrace straddles the line between the original Dutch Colonial Brooklyn towns of Brooklyn and Flatbush, as can be seen from its street grid that is bent approximately northeast–southwest along present-day Terrace Place.<ref name=":12">{{Google maps|url=https://www.google.com/maps/place/Windsor+Terrace,+Brooklyn,+NY/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x89c25b21e9b80a2d:0xb69448ccb009be06?sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwiD6uDIzdPPAhWMbD4KHRyzDbkQ8gEIfDAK|title=Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn, NY|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Old [[South Brooklyn]] (which now finds itself more westerly in disposition within the expanded boundaries of modern, consolidated Brooklyn) is located to the north of Terrace Place in the direction of 11th Avenue, and the Town of Flatbush lay to the south, located in the direction of Seeley Street. The grid of old Brooklyn, which is tilted at an angle, is adjacent to the Flatbush grid, which is roughly aligned with the [[cardinal directions]], at this juncture.<ref name=":12" /> The only other still-extant nuance of this ancient Dutch boundary is the legacy of original Catholic Parish boundaries, which are between Holy Name of Jesus to the north and Immaculate Heart of Mary to the south,<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://dioceseofbrooklyn.org/parishes/locator/|title=Parish Locator — Diocese of Brooklyn|newspaper=Diocese of Brooklyn|language=en-US|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> and [[ZIP Codes]] applied much later (11215 to the north and 11218 to the south).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/epi/Brooklyn.pdf|title=Borough of Brooklyn, New York City|website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> In this area, Vanderbilt Street, named after John Vanderbilt, splits western Brooklyn's general street grid (comprising numbered avenues from 1st–101st Streets) and southeastern Brooklyn's general street grid (comprising lettered avenues from East 1st to East 108th Streets).<ref name=":0" />

===Streets===
{{Maplink|frame=yes|zoom=14|frame-lat=40.652894|frame-long=-73.978058|coord={{Coord|40.652894|-73.978058}}|type=point|text=Street map}}

There are three streets between 16th and 17th Streets in the Windsor Terrace street grid, since the streets diverge from each other from Park Slope eastward. The northernmost of the streets is Windsor Place, which runs between 7th Avenue and Prospect Park Southwest. The southernmost of the streets is Prospect Avenue, which continues southward to Ocean Parkway (near the Fort Hamilton Parkway overpass across the Prospect Expressway) and northward to [[Third Avenue (Brooklyn)|Third Avenue]]. Running between these two streets from 10th Avenue to Terrace Place, Sherman Street is named after [[Roger Sherman]], a signatory of the [[Declaration and Resolves of the First Continental Congress|Declaration of Colonial Rights]], the [[United States Declaration of Independence]], the [[Articles of Confederation]], and the [[United States Constitution]].<ref name=":18">{{cite web|url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2009/02/windsor-terrace/|title=WINDSOR TERRACE — Forgotten New York|date=February 1, 2009|website=forgotten-ny.com|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> The street name "Windsor Place" has been applied to two different streets throughout the neighborhood's history. The current Windsor Place was formerly Braxton Street before the 1900s, while 16th Street between Prospect Park W and Prospect Park SW was known as "Windsor Place" before then.<ref name=":19">{{cite web|url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2016/10/windsor-place-park-slope-windsor-terrace/|title=WINDSOR PLACE, Park Slope & Windsor Terrace — Forgotten New York|website=forgotten-ny.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref>

Prospect Park West takes the place of 9th Avenue in the Windsor Terrace grid, and continues with the "Prospect Park West" name south of Prospect Park's borders, continuing southeastward to Green-Wood Cemetery, where it ends in a cul-de-sac.<ref name=":20" /> The stretch of Prospect Park West between 16th Street and Green-Wood Cemetery has always been called the same name as the stretch adjoining Prospect Park; the entire street was formerly and officially named 9th Avenue.<ref name=":20" />

Southeast of Prospect Park West, past [[#Bartel-Pritchard Square|Bartel-Pritchard Square]], 15th Street becomes Prospect Park Southwest. The road bends noticeably between 11th Avenue and 16th Street; Prospect Park Southwest was previously known as [[Coney Island Avenue]] and originally known as the "Coney Island Plank Road" in the days of unpaved roads, when logs or "planks" were laid for stability and to keep the mud down. The southernmost stretch of Prospect Park Southwest, south of the bend at the termination of 16th Street, still retains Coney Island Avenue's street numbering system.<ref name=":20" />

Prospect Avenue extends from Hamilton Avenue to Ocean Parkway and is crossed by a bridge at Seeley Street. The northern part was originally known as Middle Street and had its southernmost limit at what is now Terrace Place. An attempt was made in 1865 to change the name of Middle Street to Sterling Street,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/49681920/|title=Common Council|date=June 7, 1865|page=4|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=April 27, 2020|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> possibly for [[William Alexander, Lord Stirling|Lord Stirling]], but was vetoed by Mayor [[Alfred M. Wood]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/49682068/|title=The Re-naming and Re-numbering Streets Job Squelched|date=June 20, 1865|page=2|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=April 27, 2020|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> Prospect Park's establishment required additional access, and in 1868 the [[New York Legislature]] passed an act that provided for Middle Street's renaming to Prospect Avenue and its widening from {{convert|60|to|80|feet}}.<ref>{{cite book | author=New York (State) | title=Statutes at Large of the State of New York | issue=v. 7 | year=1870 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z1oSAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA292 | access-date=April 27, 2020 |at=p. 292; "Laws of 1868, Chapter 844"}}</ref> Maps made in 1874 for the Kings County Town Survey Commission provided for a {{convert|100|ft|m|adj=mid|-wide}} extension of Prospect Avenue into the [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Town of Flatbush]]; however, this was stymied by a steep, boulder-strewn [[terminal moraine]], and the fact that the city of Brooklyn's and town of Flatbush's sections of the road were misaligned. In 1903, plans were approved to correct the misalignment; Prospect Avenue was extended through the cut, and Seely Street was placed over Prospect Avenue on a concrete-and-steel arch bridge.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/49682476/|title=From East River to Ocean|date=April 12, 1903|page=54|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=April 27, 2020|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref>

====Co-named streets====
16th Street is co-named "Captain Vincent E. Brunton Way" after a [[New York City Fire Department]] captain who died in the [[September 11 attacks]]. 10th Avenue is also co-named "John P. Devaney Boulevard" in this area<ref name=":20" /> after a firefighter who died while trying to rescue residents of a burning [[Red Hook, Brooklyn|Red Hook]] building in 1989.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/02/04/nyregion/firefighter-dies-as-he-searches-for-fire-victims.html|title=Firefighter Dies As He Searches For Fire Victims|last=Lyall|first=Sarah|date=February 4, 1989|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref>

====Traffic circles====
[[Traffic circle]]s are relatively rare in New York City, but Windsor Terrace has three of them, all framing Prospect Park entrances along the park's border. The northernmost, a medium-sized traffic circle named Bartel-Pritchard Square, is at the intersection of Prospect Park West, Prospect Park Southwest, and 15th Street, and contains an ornate entrance framed with two columns.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":20" /> Another traffic circle was built at Prospect Park Southwest and 16th Street, although it no longer operates as a circle.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":20" /> The southernmost, a large traffic circle named Park Circle, is at the convergence of Prospect Park Southwest, Coney Island Avenue, Parkside Avenue, [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]], and Fort Hamilton Parkway,<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":20" /> and was reconstructed in 2010.<ref name=":22">{{cite web|url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/ssi10-parkcircle.pdf|title=Park Circle|date=2010|website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Transportation]]|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> Park Circle's entrance to Prospect Park is designed in a style similar to the Bartel-Pritchard Square entrance.<ref name=":22" />

==Demographics==
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Windsor Terrace was 20,988, an increase of 209 (1.0%) from the 20,779 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|322.38|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|65.1|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 64.9% (13,616) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 6.2% (1,298) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.1% (31) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 9.9% (2,076) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (0) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.7% (151) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 2.5% (531) from two or more races. ==Culture==
[[File:Church of the Holy Apostles Windsor Terrace.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|left|The Episcopal Church of the Holy Apostles on Greenwood Avenue]][[File:Immaculate Heart of Mary Roman Catholic Church Brooklyn from front.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.2|Immaculate Heart of Mary Church]]
Windsor Terrace is home to mainly [[Irish-American|Irish]]-, [[German-American|German]]-, [[Polish-American|Polish]]-, and [[Italian-American]] families,<ref name=":14">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newsday.com/news/new-york/city-living-windsor-terrace-m40922|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161012080028/https://www.newsday.com/news/new-york/city-living-windsor-terrace-1.2426267|url-status=live|archive-date=October 12, 2016|title=City Living: Windsor Terrace|last=Fishman|first=Levi Gibian|date=November 3, 2010|newspaper=Newsday|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> many having settled in its brick row and wood-frame houses when the neighborhood was first developed.<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}} The overwhelming majority of residents – many of whom can trace their family histories in Windsor Terrace back multiple generations – are Irish-American.<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}}<ref name=":1" /> They are traditionally affiliated with either Holy Name Church and School (the church having been built in 1874 and the school having been built in 1923,<ref name=":20" /> both located on present-day Prospect Park W),<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|2}}<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thecatholicdirectory.com/directory.cfm?fuseaction=display_site_info&siteid=52963|title=Holy Name of Jesus Parish at 245 Prospect Park West, Brooklyn, New York 11215 (Kings County) (Filtered by: 11215) United States|website=www.thecatholicdirectory.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> or Immaculate Heart of Mary (located on Fort Hamilton Parkway in Windsor Terrace's southeastern extremity).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thecatholicdirectory.com/directory.cfm?fuseaction=display_site_info&siteid=52970|title=Immaculate Heart of Mary Parish at 2805 Fort Hamiliton Parkway, Brooklyn, New York 11218 (Kings County) (Filtered by: 11218) United States|website=www.thecatholicdirectory.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Other smaller Protestant denominations exist nearby, such as the Memorial Baptist Church at 16th Street and [[Eighth Avenue (Brooklyn)|8th Avenue]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycago.org/Organs/Bkln/html/MemorialBapt.html|title=Memorial Baptist Church — Brooklyn, NY|website=www.nycago.org|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> and Holy Apostles Episcopal on Greenwood Avenue.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://nycago.org/Organs/Bkln/html/HolyApostlesEpis.html|title=Church of the Holy Apostles, Episcopal — Brooklyn, NY|website=nycago.org|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Over time, Windsor Terrace has become increasingly diverse, as [[Greeks|Greek]] and [[Hispanic]] residents have moved in. There is also a minority of [[Syria]]ns, [[Maronite]] [[Lebanese people|Lebanese]], and [[Jewish-American]]s.<ref name=":10" /><ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /><ref name=":14" /> The local synagogue is the Chabad Jewish Center.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chabadparkslope.com/templates/articlecco_cdo/aid/883807/jewish/Chabad-Windsor-Terrace.htm|title=Chabad Windsor Terrace — Chabad of Park Slope|website=www.chabadparkslope.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> There is also a newer place of worship, the Calvary Cathedral of Praise at Caton Place and East Eighth Street.<ref name=":0" />

By the 2000s and 2010s, an influx of residents seeking affordable family housing had pushed property prices up.<ref name=":10" /> In 2015, houses in various parts of Windsor Terrace sold for about $1.2 million to $2 million in 2015, and apartments cost from $400,000 for a one-bedroom apartment to more than $1 million for a three-bedroom apartment.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015">{{cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/windsor-terrace-grows-livelier-but-more-expensive-1433543463|title=Windsor Terrace Grows Livelier, but More Expensive|last=Lefkowitz|first=Melanie|date=June 5, 2015|website=WSJ|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Windsor Terrace is becoming more ethnically diverse and culturally active, owing to a demographic change since the 1990s, when the area had a more elderly population and not as many families with young children. The increased presence of many families with young kids has not indicated a significant cultural change in the neighborhood.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" />

However, despite the increased population, the area still maintains a bit of small-town atmosphere, with relatively low house turnover. A real estate broker who grew up in the area said that in Windsor Terrace, "everybody says hello" to each other,<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /> and a real-estate feature in ''[[The New York Times]]'' stated that "residents look out for one another at all hours of the day."<ref name=":10" /> There is more on-street vehicle parking in Windsor Terrace than in nearby, more populous neighborhoods.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /> The area's lack of [[traffic light]]s, due to low traffic volumes, make Windsor Terrace feel like a small town, as do well-maintained one-family houses, some with covered balconies and [[stained glass]] windows; other houses with "[[bay window]]s, both rounded and faceted"; and yet other "clapboard [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]]" houses with multicolored [[cornice]]s.<ref name=":10" /> There are a few apartment buildings, including Windsor Tower, a 10-story building that was downgraded from 22 stories after community objections;<ref name=":10" /> a 73-unit, seven-floor rental building that opened in 2015;<ref name=":10" /> and a [[condominium]] tower at 279 Prospect Park W, a former paint factory storage building that posed as a bank in the 1975 movie ''[[Dog Day Afternoon]]''.<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name=":10" /> The houses are of varying types, including some small one-story clapboard houses that have attics and date to the neighborhood's development; larger two-story houses with basements and some wood framing on the exterior; and attached brick [[townhouse]]s with either flat facades with normal-sized windows or curved facades with bay windows, both with two floors and a [[basement]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":19" />

The neighborhood is mostly residential, with some commerce along Prospect Park W, Prospect Avenue, and Fort Hamilton Parkway. The latter two corridors have seen an increased commercial presence since the 2000s, but these new stores are mostly [[Family business|family-owned businesses]], with the exception of a [[Walgreens]] and a grocery store in the area.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /> There are at least four bars (The renown Farrell's Bar & Grill, the Double Windsor, and the Adirondack) as well as a combination cafe and food store called The Tuscan Gun; a combination pub and restaurant called Hamilton's; a French restaurant called Le Paddock; and a Middle Eastern restaurant called Batata.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /> The commercial streets are also lined with new "coffee shops, yoga studios and vegetarian restaurants" that have popped up since the area's gentrification.<ref name=":10" />

==Police and crime==
Windsor Terrace is patrolled by the 72nd Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 830 4th Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 72nd Precinct">{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/72nd-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 72nd Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 72nd Precinct ranked 16th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010. Total crime has decreased since the 1990s, and the 72nd Precinct is one of the safest precincts in Brooklyn {{as of|2010|lc=y}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/sunset-park/|title=Windsor Terrace & Sunset Park – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-date=March 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306043630/https://www.dnainfo.com/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/sunset-park/|url-status=dead}}</ref> The 72nd Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 79.1% between 1990 and 2018. The precinct reported 2 murders, 32 rapes, 185 robberies, 209 felony assaults, 153 burglaries, 468 grand larcenies, and 77 grand larcenies auto in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-072pct.pdf|title=72nd Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

Windsor Terrace is a heavily [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] area; in the 2016 Presidential election, 84% of the 9th Congressional district (where Windsor Terrace had been located from 2013 until 2022) voted for Hillary Clinton, compared to 15% for rival [[Donald Trump]]. In the [[New York Democratic primary, 2016|2016 Democratic presidential primary]], [[Hillary Clinton]] narrowly won the primary in Windsor Terrace, receiving 2,756 votes ({{Percentage|2756|5324|1}}) to [[Bernie Sanders]]'s 2,568 votes ({{Percentage|2568|5324|1}}) with a total of 5,324 Democrats voting.<ref>Matthew Bloch & Wilson Andrews, [https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/04/19/us/elections/new-york-city-democratic-primary-results.html How Every New York City Neighborhood Voted in the Democratic Primary], ''New York Times'' (April 20, 2016).</ref> Windsor Terrace had relatively few Republican primary voters. Just 371 voters cast ballots in the [[New York Republican primary, 2016|2016 Republican primary]], with 197 people ({{percentage|197|371|1}} of the Republican electorate in the neighborhood) voting for [[Donald Trump]], 120 for [[John Kasich]] ({{percentage|120|371|1}} of the Republican electorate), and 54 for [[Ted Cruz]] ({{percentage|54|371|1}} of the Republican electorate).<ref>Matthew Bloch & Wilson Andrews, [https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/04/19/us/elections/new-york-city-democratic-primary-results.html How Every New York City Neighborhood Voted in the Republican Primary], ''New York Times'' (April 20, 2016).</ref>

===Schools===
The neighborhood public elementary schools, PS 154 (The Windsor Terrace School) on 11th Avenue and PS 130 (The Parkside School) on Ocean Avenue, are well regarded. Each school features a number of enrichment programs for students, such as chess and journalism.<ref>Hemphill, Clara ''New York City’s Best Public Elementary Schools: A Parent’s Guide, Third Edition'', Teacher’s College Press, 2005, {{ISBN|978-0-8077-4613-4}}</ref> In 2013–2014, 64% of PS 154 students met or exceeded [[Common Core State Standards Initiative|Common Core]] standards in the [[Language arts|English Language Arts]] (ELA) exams and 65% met or exceeded the standards on the math exams. At PS 130, 32% of ELA test-takers met or exceeded standards, and 41% did so on the math test.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /> For the 2017–18 school year, PS 154 placed in the top 30% of all schools in New York for overall test scores (math proficiency is top 30%, and reading proficiency is top 20%). The percentage of students achieving proficiency in math was 77% (the New York state average was 52%) and the percentage of students achieving proficiency in reading/language arts was 82% (the New York state average was 52%).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.publicschoolreview.com/windsor-terrace-school-profile |title=Windsor Terrace School (2022 Ranking) | Brooklyn, NY |publisher=Publicschoolreview.com |date= |accessdate=January 10, 2022}}</ref> PS 130 placed in the top 50% of all schools in New York for overall test scores (math proficiency was top 50%, and reading proficiency was top 50%) for the 2017–18 school year. The percentage of students achieving proficiency in math was 62% and the percentage of students achieving proficiency in reading/language arts was 58%.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.publicschoolreview.com/p-s-130-parkside-profile |title=P.S. 130 Parkside (2022 Ranking) | Brooklyn, NY |publisher=Publicschoolreview.com |date= |accessdate=January 10, 2022}}</ref>

The NYCDOE district in which the schools are operated, District 15, was rezoned in 2014 due to an increased enrollment in the two schools; some students formerly zoned to PS 154 are now zoned to PS 130.<ref name="Lefkowitz 2015" /><ref name="Albrecht 20142">{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20141028/windsor-terrace/parents-say-proposed-district-15-rezoning-forces-students-travel-too-far|title=Parents Say Proposed District 15 Rezoning Forces Students to Travel Too Far|last=Albrecht|first=Leslie|date=October 28, 2014|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=October 11, 2016|archive-date=October 11, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011142234/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20141028/windsor-terrace/parents-say-proposed-district-15-rezoning-forces-students-travel-too-far|url-status=dead}}</ref> This rezoning proved contentious, with some rezoned students' parents saying that the rezoning requires some students to travel over {{Convert|0.5|mi|km}} across "two highways" to get to school.<ref name="Albrecht 20142" /> In addition, since the rezoning, PS 154 has seen an increase in enrollment despite its decreased student catchment area; in 2016–2017, the school had its first-ever student [[Wait list|waiting list]], amid cuts to the school's [[pre-kindergarten]] program.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160317/windsor-terrace/windsor-terraces-ps-154-has-first-ever-waitlist-even-after-zone-shrinks|title=Windsor Terrace's P.S. 154 Has First Ever Waitlist Even After Zone Shrinks|last=Albrecht|first=Leslie|date=March 17, 2016|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=October 11, 2016|archive-date=October 11, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011142808/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160317/windsor-terrace/windsor-terraces-ps-154-has-first-ever-waitlist-even-after-zone-shrinks|url-status=dead}}</ref> There is also another public school nearby, PS 295 on 18th Street in Park Slope, to accommodate extra students from Windsor Terrace.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://schools.nyc.gov/SchoolPortals/15/K295/default.htm|title=Welcome — P.S. 295 - K295|date=October 10, 2016|website=New York City Department of Education|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> In the 2012–2013 NYCDOE Progress Report, this school received an "A," garnering a quality score of 60.2 out of 100.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://schools.nyc.gov/OA/SchoolReports/2012-13/Progress_Report_2013_EMS_K295.pdf|title=Progress Report 2012-13 K295|date=2013|website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Education]]|access-date=October 10, 2016}}</ref>

MS 839, serving grades 6–8, is located at 713 Caton Avenue.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.schools.nyc.gov/schools/K839|title=M.S. 839|website=www.schools.nyc.gov|access-date=February 22, 2020}}</ref> [[Brooklyn College Academy]] operates an annex site for freshmen and sophomore high school students at 350 Coney Island Avenue, with the juniors' and seniors' building at [[Brooklyn College]].<ref name=":10" />

The St. Joseph the Worker Catholic Academy opened in 2012. This [[Catholic school]] is a consolidation of Holy Name of Jesus and Immaculate Heart of Mary's elementary schools into Holy Name's existing infrastructure on 9th Avenue, offering Pre-K(3) to 8th Grade, including Honors Classes and after school programs.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.optionc.com/Templates/CTPrayer/statement.asp?key=866&section=schoolinfo|title=St Joseph the Worker Catholic Academy|website=www.optionc.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Another Catholic school, [[Bishop Ford Central Catholic High School|Bishop Ford High School]], formerly operated at 500 19th Street in Windsor Terrace from 1952 to 2014. |access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> The latter station, Fort Hamilton Parkway, has a long passageway due to its unusual location under the [[Prospect Expressway]]; its three entrances (one on Fort Hamilton Parkway itself, and two on Prospect Avenue) straddle the expressway, which splits the neighborhood in two.<ref name=":18" />

[[MTA Regional Bus Operations]] operates [[bus]] routes in the area. {{As of|2016}}, there are four local bus routes: the [[B61 (New York City bus)|B61]], [[B67 (New York City bus)|B67]], [[B68 (New York City bus)|B68]], and [[B69 (New York City bus)|B69]]. Several [[List of express bus routes in New York City|express buses]] and the [[B103 (New York City bus)|B103 Limited]] bus pass through Windsor Terrace without stopping.<ref name="MTA-BrooklynBusMap-Current">{{Cite NYC bus map|B}}</ref>

As elsewhere in Brooklyn, [[tram|trolley]] service, operated by the [[Rapid transit operations of the BRT and BMT|BMT's rapid transit arm]], ran in the neighborhood well into the 1950s and early '60s. The Seventh Avenue Line (now the B67 bus route) was converted from trolley to bus operations in 1951,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/56107825/?terms=%22seventh%2Bavenue%22%2Bomnibus|title=Public Notices|date=January 4, 1951|work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]]|access-date=October 10, 2016|via=[[newspapers.com]]}}</ref> and a year later, the Vanderbilt Avenue Line (now the B69) was similarly converted.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/52898426/|title=Board of Estimate Notice of Public Hearing|date=July 12, 1951|work=[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]]|access-date=October 10, 2016|via=[[newspapers.com]]}}</ref> A trolley barn, located between Green-Wood Cemetery and the Prospect Expressway, formerly served the [[Culver Line (surface)|Culver]] and [[Crosstown Line (Brooklyn surface)|Crosstown]] trolley lines on a site where a former federal prison was located during the [[American Civil War]]. It was replaced in 1962 by the Bishop Ford High School.<ref name=":0" />

The Prospect Expressway, built between 1953 and 1960, runs through the middle of the neighborhood, with the majority of the neighborhood northeast of the expressway, and a small part of the neighborhood in the southwest connected by various bridges to the northeast section. Some neighborhood streets, such as Greenwood Avenue and Vanderbilt Place, were bisected by the expressway and remain so, while others, such as Seeley Street, 11th Avenue/Terrace Place, and Prospect Park W, are bridged over the highway.<ref name=":1" /> A plan to extend the highway along Ocean Parkway was never realized, though Ocean Parkway serves as a [[Frontage road|service road]] for the expressway for a short distance in southern Windsor Terrace. In the late 1950s, the Holy Name of Jesus Church led a failed effort to try to reroute the Prospect Expressway elsewhere or cancel the expressway altogether.<ref name=":1" />

{{anchor|Kensington Stables}}Kensington Stables is the only remaining [[stable]] near Prospect Park. In the days where horse stables saw a lot of business, there were many dozens of stables in the area.<ref name=":0" /> The barn was built in 1930 as the last extension of the riding academy at 11 Ocean Parkway, 57 Caton Place (built in 1917).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":17">[http://www.nycgovparks.org/facilities/horseback "Horseback Riding"] on the [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] website</ref>  The original riding academy closed in 1937 and is now a warehouse.<ref name=":17" /> By around the 1940s, the stables started to disappear, with some being converted into [[Bowling|bowling alleys]] or [[Roller rink|roller skating rinks]], and others just disappearing.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/06/11/nyregion/thecity/11stab.html|title=When the Horsemen Passed By|last=Berger|first=Paul|date=June 11, 2006|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Today, Kensington Stables gives lessons in The Shoe in Prospect Park.<ref name=":17" /> Kensington Stables now exists on the Windsor Terrace side of the border between Kensington and Windsor Terrace.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/hpd/html/buyers/nychome-neighborhoods-brooklyn-kensington.shtml "Kensington Real Estate"] on NYC.gov</ref>

[[Bartel-Pritchard Square|{{Anchor|Bartel-Pritchard Square}}Bartel-Pritchard Square]], in Windsor Terrace's northern extremity, is a traffic circle at the intersection of Prospect Park West, 15th Street, and Prospect Park Southwest. Its name commemorates local residents, Emil Bartel and William Pritchard, who died during [[World War I]] while in combat.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":20" /> The circle, which was dedicated under its current name in 1922,<ref name="Berenson DeMause 2001 p. 48">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xDkdA2Yi7swC&pg=PA48|title=The Complete Illustrated Guidebook to Prospect Park and the Brooklyn Botanic Garden|last1=Berenson|first1=R.J.|last2=DeMause|first2=N.|publisher=Silver Lining Books|year=2001|isbn=978-0-7607-2213-8|page=48|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> originally had a flower garden in its center.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160304/windsor-terrace/how-bartel-pritchard-square-got-its-name-despite-being-circle-shaped|title=How Bartel-Pritchard 'Square' Got Its Name Despite Being Circle-Shaped|last=Levy|first=Nicole|date=March 4, 2016|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=October 11, 2016|archive-date=October 11, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011224216/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160304/windsor-terrace/how-bartel-pritchard-square-got-its-name-despite-being-circle-shaped|url-status=dead}}</ref> A black granite monument in the center of the circle—installed in 1965 as a result of a donation by the Patrick J. Devaney Post #964, [[Veterans of Foreign Wars|VFW]] of the U.S.—memorializes all of the locals who have died in war.<ref name=":20" /><ref name=":21" /> One side has the inscription "In memory of the men / of this community who / have given their lives / In wartime service/ to their country / Erected by / Patrick J. Devaney Post #964 / V.F.W. of U.S. / 1965" while the other side has the inscription "For Valor / and / Sacrifice / 1965".<ref name=":21">{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/bartel-pritchard-square/monuments/80|title=Bartel-Pritchard Square Monuments — Bartel-Pritchard Circle War Memorial : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org|access-date=October 10, 2016}}</ref> Like similar structures such as [[Times Square]] and [[Herald Square]], the Bartel-Pritchard Square is geometrically not a square, despite its name.<ref name=":2" /> The park entrance adjoining Bartel–Pritchard Square is shaped as a gateway between two [[Stanford White]]-designed granite pillars with "what appears to be huge bronze lanterns" adorning the pillars' apexes. The pillars, which are based on [[Dancers of Delphi|an acanthus column in Delphi with sculptures on top]], were unveiled in 1906, shortly after White had died.<ref name="Berenson DeMause 2001 p. 48" />

[[File:Prospect Park Bartel-Pritchard Circle Columns.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|left|The columns at the park entrance outside Bartel-Pritchard Square]]

Since at least 1908, Windsor Terrace has had its own [[movie theater]] since the Marathon Theatre opened at present-day 188 Prospect Park W in 1908.<ref name=":4">{{cite web|url=http://cinematreasures.org/theaters/21858|title=Marathon Theater in Brooklyn, NY — Cinema Treasures|website=cinematreasures.org|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{cite web|url=http://cinematreasures.org/theaters/1268|title=Pavilion Theatre in Brooklyn, NY — Cinema Treasures|website=cinematreasures.org|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> The 500-seat<ref name=":0" /> Marathon Theatre had a [[Wurlitzer]] organ installed in 1927, shortly before its 1928 demolition.<ref name=":4" /> In August of that year, the 1,516-seat, [[Art Deco]] Sanders Theatre was opened on the site of the former Marathon Theatre, where it operated for half a century before its closure in 1976. The building stood vacant for twenty years after that,<ref name=":5" /> and investors bought the building in 1993 in hopes of reopening the theater.<ref name=":0" /> The Pavilion Theatre, a 3-screen news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/boroughs/aisles-joy-coming-life-article-1.748651|title=AISLES OF JOY COMING TO LIFE|last=Hamill|first=Denis|date=July 26, 1996|newspaper=NY Daily floors,<ref name=":8" /> as well as a rumor of bedbug-infested upholstery<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gothamist.com/2010/07/19/park_slope_movie_theater_spraying_f.php|title=Bedbugs II Screening at Park Slope Pavilion?|last=Del Signore|first=John|date=July 19, 2010|website=Gothamist|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> and malfunctions in the theater's heating system.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/brooklyn/pavilion-cinema-heating-malfunction-leaves-customers-big-chill-article-1.1527789|title=Pavilion Cinema heating malfunction leaves customers with 'Big Chill'|last1=Sandoval|first1=Edgar|date=November 21, 2013|last2=Yaniv|first2=Oren|newspaper=NY Daily News|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> In October 2016, the building was closed in preparation for conversion to a 7-screen, 650-seat theater.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":8" /> Operated by [[Nitehawk Cinema]], the refurbished Pavilion Theatre, where patrons would be able to dine and url=https://brooklyneagle.com/articles/2018/12/19/photos-nitehawk-cinema-finally-opens-in-park-slopes-landmarked-pavilion-theater/ | access-date=October 11, 2019}}</ref>

[[Farrell's Bar & Grill]], at 16th Street and Prospect Park W, is a noted community institution that has been continuously run by three owners since 1933.<ref name="brookneighb" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/02/16/nyregion/at-a-famous-brooklyn-oasis-parched-throats-find-a-dry-spell.html|title=At a Famous Brooklyn Oasis, Parched Throats Find a Dry Spell|last=Confessore|first=Nicholas|date=February 16, 2006|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> Famous among the fire and police officers who live in the community,<ref name=":7" /> it is said to be one of the first bars in New York City to get its liquor license at the end of [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]].<ref name=":9">{{cite web|url=http://www.bkmag.com/2015/06/01/all-in-the-family-farrells-bar-and-grill/|title=All in the Family: Farrell's Bar and Grill|last=Gharib|first=Ali|date=June 1, 2015|website=Brooklyn Magazine|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> It has been used as a standard bar backdrop in many film sequences. The neighborhood legend persists that until 1971, when [[Shirley MacLaine]] and [[Pete Hamill]] went into the bar during the filming of ''[[Desperate Characters (film)|Desperate Characters]]'' and successfully demanded that MacLaine be served from the bar; until that time, Farrell's only served men at the bar and women at the rear of the establishment.<ref name=":0" /> Farrell's, which known for being open every day from 10 a.m. to 3 a.m., was closed for a nine-day renovation in 2006, marking the bar's longest duration of closure since Prohibition ended.<ref name=":7" /> Its iconic [[styrofoam cup]]s filled with beer,<ref name=":14" /> a tradition since its cardboard "containers" were replaced by Styrofoam "containers" in 1985, were discontinued in 2015 following a citywide ban on Styrofoam food implements.<ref name=":9" />

Due to Windsor Terrace's topography, there is a [[terminal moraine]] that ends in Windsor Terrace, creating a steep slope. As a result, at the location where the intersection of Seeley Street and Prospect Avenue would have been; Seeley Street uses a [[Arch bridge|concrete arch bridge]] that spans {{Height|ft=8|in=7}} above Prospect Avenue.<ref name=":18" /> The {{Convert|143.7
|ft|m|adj=on}} bridge<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bridgehunter.com/ny/kings/2244470/|title=Seeley Street Bridge|website=Bridgehunter.com|access-date=October 11, 2016}}</ref> was built by 1903 at a cost of $22,000,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/53925577/?terms=seeley%2Bstreet%2Bbridge|title=Seeley Street Bridge - 12 April 1903|date=April 12, 1903|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|page=54|access-date=October 11, 2016|via=[[newspapers.com]]}}</ref> and is supported by underpinning since the IND subway runs under Prospect Avenue at this point.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/59900872/?terms=seeley%2Bstreet%2Bbridge|title=Underpin Seeley Street Bridge for Subway|date=May 24, 1930|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|page=3|access-date=October 11, 2016|via=[[newspapers.com]]}}</ref> While street bridges that span other streets are more common in the hilly [[The Bronx|Bronx]], they are rare in Brooklyn.<ref name=":1" /> This particular bridge does not appear on contemporary maps.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2016/04/seeley-feel-me-windsor-terrace/|title=SEELEY, FEEL ME, Windsor Terrace — Forgotten New York|date=April 22, 2016|website=forgotten-ny.com|access-date=October 12, 2016}}</ref> The bridge has a stairway on its side that connects the two streets.<ref name=":18" />
